description: Width tiers for English Year 7 — all 24 descriptors across Language, Literature and Literacy strands
subject: English

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest context in which a student honestly satisfies the descriptor's command term. For Language concept standards (understand, identify, recognise): minimum is one text type or one example set. For Literacy capability standards (analyse, explain, create): minimum is one task context. For Literature standards: minimum is one text.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope as ACARA intended — grounded in the most common elaboration cases. For Language standards: the range of text types and language examples the descriptor covers. For Literacy capabilities: a range of task contexts that builds transferable skill. For Literature: engagement across more than one text or context.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add phenomena, text types, cultural contexts or task variants — not harder versions of the same context. First Nations Australian text and language contexts are included as default wider directions where elaborations indicate them.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations are used as source data to ground typical_width and identify wider directions. Not every elaboration becomes a tier item — where elaborations are variants of the same activity they are merged. Wider may reasonably extend beyond elaborations where the direction is clearly within the descriptor's territory and year band.

AC9E7LA01.minimum_width: Identify two examples of language use (vocabulary, idiom, register or dialect) that signal something about a speaker's or writer's personal or social identity; explain what each signals.
AC9E7LA01.typical_width: Examine how language expresses and creates personal and social identity across a range of contexts — local idioms and community belonging, dialogue that reveals character in comics or animations, code-switching across social contexts — and explain how language both reflects and constructs who a person is perceived to be.
wider: Investigate how names, titles and honorifics create social identity and position relationships — compare examples across cultures or communities
Examine how the same person uses language differently across social contexts (family, peers, teachers) and discuss what the variation reveals about shifting identities
Explore how First Nations Australian language features — including specific vocabulary, address terms and relational language — express cultural identity and community belonging
elaborations: understanding local idioms and discussing their connection with personal and social identities
developing dialogue that reveals character in comics, cartoons and animations

AC9E7LA02.minimum_width: In a given text, identify two words or phrases that express evaluation; classify each as emotional response, judgement or aesthetic appreciation; identify one evaluative claim and note whether it is supported by textual reference or assertion.
AC9E7LA02.typical_width: Examine evaluative language across the three domains (affect, judgement, appreciation) in a range of texts; analyse how evaluations of narrative and persuasive texts are substantiated by textual reference and external sources; recognise how evaluative language critically assesses evidence reliability.
wider: Compare evaluative vocabulary in a student review and a published critic's review of the same text — examine how vocabulary choice signals authority and register
Examine how evaluative language is used to assess source reliability and evidence validity in informational and media texts, not just literary texts
Analyse how evaluative language choices differ when the same text is reviewed for different audiences — what shifts in the vocabulary of affect, judgement and appreciation?
elaborations: building knowledge about words of evaluation, including words to express emotional responses to texts, judgement of characters and their actions, and appreciation of the aesthetic qualities of text
analysing how evaluative language can be used to assess the qualities of a narrative or persuasive text; for example, its impact on the reader or the author's skill in the use of language
recognising how evaluative language is used to critically assess the validity of evidence and the reliability of sources

AC9E7LA03.minimum_width: Compare two texts with different purposes; identify one structural difference and one language feature difference; explain how each serves its respective purpose.
AC9E7LA03.typical_width: Examine how text structure and language features vary systematically across a range of text types — book and film reviews (context → summary → judgement), persuasive texts (social purpose reflected in structure and language), literary texts, arguments, discussions and analytical responses — and describe how structure and language serve each purpose.
wider: Analyse the structure and language features of advertising posters as persuasive texts — examine how visual and verbal language work together to serve purpose
Compare how the same subject is structured and written differently for different text types (e.g. a news report, an opinion piece and a social media post on the same event)
Examine texts about First Nations Australian histories and cultures across different text types and discuss how structure and language feature choices reflect the purpose and audience of each
elaborations: examining the structures of book or film reviews and how they might move from description of context to summary of the text and then to judgement of the text

recognising the social purpose of a persuasive text and how the purpose is reflected in the text structure and by the language features; for example, analysing the structure and language features of advertising posters

describing the structure and language features of literary texts, arguments, discussions, creative and analytical responses to literary texts, films or popular media, and discussing how the structure and language serves the purpose of the text

AC9E7LA04.minimum_width: In a given text, identify the topic sentence of two paragraphs and the overview or introductory paragraph; explain what job each does in guiding the reader.
AC9E7LA04.typical_width: Examine how cohesion devices — topic sentences, sentence openers, text connectives, overviews, initial and concluding paragraphs — work as a system to guide readers through a text's logic; compare how these devices operate across at least two text types.
wider: Compare and analyse cohesion strategies in digital news sites and print media — how do structural devices create cohesion when texts may be read non-linearly or in fragments?
Identify how authors foreshadow text development through sentence openers and text connectives — trace the signposting across a whole text
Examine a text with weak or absent cohesion devices and explain what effect this has on readability and comprehension
elaborations: comparing and analysing the structure of media texts such as digital news sites or print media, identifying strategies used to create cohesion
identifying how authors foreshadow how a text will unfold; for example, identifying the topic sentence, sentence openers and text connectives

AC9E7LA05.minimum_width: Identify the independent and dependent clauses in a complex sentence; explain what the dependent clause adds; identify a compound-complex sentence and explain how it differs from a complex sentence.
AC9E7LA05.typical_width: Understand how complex and compound-complex sentences elaborate, extend and explain ideas; examine how sentence structure choices serve rhetorical purposes across a range of text types; explain why varying sentence structure serves a text's purpose better than using one sentence type throughout.
wider: Compare how the same idea can be expressed as complex vs compound-complex and explain what the compound-complex version adds — using the ACARA example of dinosaurs/weather/vegetation
Investigate how subordinating conjunction choice (because, although, when, so that) shapes the semantic relationship between clauses and the purpose the sentence serves
Examine published texts to find where writers use simple sentences for impact alongside complex structures — discuss how the contrast serves the text
elaborations: identifying and experimenting with a range of clause structures and discussing the effect of these in the expression and development of ideas
consolidating knowledge of simple, compound and complex sentences, recognising that a simple sentence can express sophisticated ideas and a complex sentence need not express 'complex' ideas
examining the addition of ideas using a complex-compound sentence; for example, 'When dinosaurs roamed the earth, weather patterns shifted significantly and as a result vegetation depleted.'

AC9E7LA06.minimum_width: Identify a tense inconsistency in a given sentence; explain why it creates confusion for the reader.
AC9E7LA06.typical_width: Examine how verb tense is maintained across compound, complex and compound-complex sentences; identify intentional tense shifts (flashback, quoted speech) and distinguish them from errors; apply tense consistency in own writing.
wider: Limited width — tense consistency does not vary meaningfully across contexts at this year band. The descriptor is narrow and mechanical. Extension goes further: examine how stream of consciousness or historical present deliberately violate tense consistency and discuss how context signals intentionality.
Compare how tense consistency operates differently across text types — past tense in narratives, present tense in explanations — and discuss what tense shift signals about text type
elaborations: identifying and discussing how verb tense is maintained in compound, complex and compound-complex sentences

identifying and discussing different forms of verb tenses and their use to maintain consistency of tense in different sentences; for example, 'I organise the cake stall every week, and I am running the meeting this weekend, as well.'
AC9E7LA06.width_notes: Thin width — tense consistency is a precision skill with limited contextual variation at Y7. The wider items extend conceptually rather than broadening contexts.

AC9E7LA07.minimum_width: In a given image, identify one visual technique (vector, angle or social distance) and explain what it communicates about the viewer-subject relationship.
AC9E7LA07.typical_width: Analyse how vectors, angle and social distance work together to create perspective in visual texts; compare how technique combinations create different perspectives in animations and advertisements across at least two visual text types.
wider: Analyse how illustrations in picture books, graphic novels and advertisements use size, colour, angle, proximity, vector and salience together to influence the reader — applying the full visual grammar vocabulary
Compare how different advertisements for the same product use different technique combinations to target different audiences
Examine how visual perspective techniques in First Nations Australian visual art (including contemporary digital works) create cultural meaning and position the viewer
elaborations: comparing how perspectives are created in animations and advertisements
comparing how different advertisements advertise the same product, using techniques to create different perspectives for effect
analysing how the illustrations in picture books, graphic novels and advertisements use size, colour, angle, proximity, vector and salience to influence the reader

AC9E7LA08.minimum_width: Identify three specialist or technical terms in a given text; explain why precise vocabulary is needed in that field; identify one term with both everyday and technical meanings and explain both.
AC9E7LA08.typical_width: Investigate how specialist and technical vocabulary builds knowledge across at least two subject areas; examine high-utility academic vocabulary (factor, hypothesise, issue, critique) that appears across disciplines; explore terms used to discuss a specific topic (e.g. poetic devices) and explain how technical terms enable more precise discussion.
wider: Investigate Greek and Latin roots across subject areas — how does knowing a root help decode unfamiliar technical terms in Science, Maths and English simultaneously?
Examine how the same term carries different technical meanings across disciplines (e.g. 'argument' in English vs Maths vs Philosophy) and discuss how students learn to shift between them
Explore how misunderstanding a technical term as its everyday counterpart leads to disciplinary misunderstanding — trace a specific example from a student-facing text
elaborations: recognising vocabulary used to represent high utility, abstract academic concepts; for example, 'factor', 'hypothesise', 'issue' and 'critique'
identifying vocabulary used to write about a topic; for example, using terms for poetic devices and words to explain the effects of the devices in poems

AC9E7LA09.minimum_width: Identify a colon and a bracket in given sentences; explain what each signals or adds to meaning.
AC9E7LA09.typical_width: Examine how colons introduce lists, elaborations and quotations; examine how brackets add parenthetical information (clarification, aside, example, attribution); explain how each punctuation choice affects the reader's experience of the information.
wider: Limited width — colons and brackets are a narrow punctuation set with a small number of uses. Extension goes further: compare when a writer chooses brackets vs dashes vs commas for parenthetical content, and discuss what each choice signals about the information's relationship to the main clause.
Examine how the impact of bracketed or colon-introduced information changes the meaning and rhythm of the sentence — compare versions with and without the added information
elaborations: examining the impact of information added to sentences when colons and brackets are used
AC9E7LA09.width_notes: Thin width — one elaboration, narrow mechanical scope. Wider extends by comparison with related punctuation choices rather than adding genuinely new contexts.

AC9E7LY08.minimum_width: Identify the base word or affix in an unfamiliar word and use that morphological knowledge to spell it correctly; identify one Greek or Latin root and explain how it contributes to the word's meaning.
AC9E7LY08.typical_width: Use spelling rules, base words, prefixes, suffixes and Greek and Latin roots strategically to learn and spell new words; investigate word families built from common roots across multiple subject areas; apply spelling rules governing base-word changes when suffixes are added.
wider: Investigate how Greek roots dominate scientific vocabulary while Latin roots dominate legal and academic vocabulary — explore examples across Science, Maths and English
Build a personal glossary of high-yield Greek and Latin roots encountered across subjects and use it to decode unfamiliar technical terms
Examine how First Nations Australian language words have entered Australian English — investigate etymologies and discuss what the borrowings reveal about contact history

AC9E7LY01.minimum_width: Identify one specific technology and explain one effect it has on how texts are read, created or responded to — beyond convenience, explaining how the technology changes the experience.
AC9E7LY01.typical_width: Explain how current technologies affect reading, creating and responding across multiple text types — examining communicative technologies (SMS, email, GIFs) and their influence on written language; analysing interactive elements of digital texts; identifying how technology has changed what counts as newsworthy.
wider: Investigate how algorithmic curation affects what texts readers encounter — examine how recommendation systems shape the information environment
Examine how new digital text forms (vlogs, podcasts, interactive stories) emerged from technological affordances — what does each technology enable that wasn't possible before?
Explore how First Nations Australian communities use digital technologies to create, share and preserve language and cultural texts — discuss what technologies make possible for cultural continuity
elaborations: investigating the influence of communicative technologies such as SMS, email and GIFs on written language
analysing the impact of interactive elements of digital texts on texts such as magazines read in a digital form
identifying changes in topics considered to be newsworthy as a result of technological change

AC9E7LY02.minimum_width: Participate in a discussion demonstrating at least two interaction skills; identify one feature of a spoken text and explain its effect on audience understanding or engagement.
AC9E7LY02.typical_width: Use a range of interaction skills across formal and informal discussion and presentation contexts; evaluate the features of spoken texts including evidence selection, voice features and vocabulary choices; adapt language to audience and purpose.
wider: Participate in structured debate or formal discussion and evaluate how the interaction skills required differ from informal conversation
Identify key evidence supporting an argument in a discussion between two speakers — evaluate how effectively each speaker uses evidence and interaction moves
Compare the interaction features of formal and informal spoken texts on the same topic and evaluate how language choices affect credibility and audience engagement
elaborations: participating in pair, group, class, school and/or community speaking and listening situations, including informal conversations, discussions, debates and presentations

using effective strategies for dialogue and discussion in a range of formal and informal contexts, including speaking clearly and coherently and for an appropriate length, clarifying and rephrasing comments of others
identifying key evidence supporting an argument in a discussion between 2 speakers
choosing vocabulary and sentence structures for purposes and audiences, adapting language choices to meet the perceived audience needs
ensuring that ways of communicating for particular audiences are acknowledged

AC9E7LY03.minimum_width: In a given text, identify two language features and explain how each shapes the meaning a reader constructs.
AC9E7LY03.typical_width: Analyse how language features shape meaning and vary according to audience and purpose across a range of texts — explaining the relationship between specific features and their effects; examining how features shift between texts targeting different audiences.
wider: Examine depictions of histories and cultures of First Nations Australians in texts and discuss how language features shape the meaning constructed about those histories and cultures
Analyse how the same event is represented differently in texts for different audiences (news article, social media post, children's explanation) — trace how language feature choices differ and why
Examine how language features in advertising texts position a specific target audience — identify the audience and justify by tracing specific feature choices
elaborations: explaining the relationship between language features, and audience and purpose, such as identifying which group would be the most likely target audience for the information in an advertisement and justifying why
examining depictions of the histories and cultures of First Nations Australians, discussing language features that shape meaning

AC9E7LY04.minimum_width: In a given text, identify the idea structure being used (taxonomy, cause-effect, extended metaphor or chronology) and explain how it organises the information.
AC9E7LY04.typical_width: Explain how idea structures serve different purposes across text types — taxonomies in explanations, cause-effect in arguments, extended metaphors in literary and persuasive texts, chronology in recounts; examine how the same idea structure can serve different purposes in different contexts.
wider: Examine how cause-effect structure is used not just to explain but to persuade — trace how a causal chain constructs a recommended action as inevitable
Compare how the same sequence of events can be structured as chronology (neutral recount) or cause-effect (persuasive argument) and discuss how structure choice shapes interpretation
Analyse how extended metaphors in First Nations Australian texts organise ideas and carry cultural meaning — examine how the metaphorical framework shapes understanding
elaborations: identifying cause and effect in explanations and how these are used to convince an audience of a course of action

AC9E7LY05.minimum_width: Identify a point in a text where meaning is implied rather than stated and explain the inferential reasoning; determine the key idea of a given paragraph and write a one-sentence summary.
AC9E7LY05.typical_width: Apply comprehension strategies including inferring, predicting, connecting and summarising to analyse and summarise information and ideas across a range of text types; determine and summarise key ideas at paragraph and chapter level in extended texts.
wider: Analyse visual features including choice of image, colour, composition and font in covers of different editions of books — explain what inferences about tone, genre and audience each cover invites
Compare the presentation of ideas in formal and informal speeches and determine the key ideas in each — discuss why the same ideas may be summarised differently depending on context
Apply comprehension strategies to multimodal texts — explain how strategies like inferring and connecting operate differently when meaning is distributed across image, sound and text
elaborations: comparing the presentation of ideas in formal and informal speeches and determining the reasons for the differences
analysing visual features including choice of image, colour, composition and font in covers of different editions of books when predicting the tone of a text
determining and summarising the key idea(s) of paragraphs and chapters in an extended text

AC9E7LY06.minimum_width: Create a written or multimodal text for a given purpose; identify two deliberate structural or language choices made during drafting and explain what each contributes to the purpose.
AC9E7LY06.typical_width: Plan, create, edit and publish written and multimodal texts across at least two purposes (imaginative, reflective, informative, persuasive or analytical); make deliberate selections of text structures, language features and literary devices; edit for meaning by varying sentence structures, adding or substituting words for impact, and reviewing grammar and punctuation.
wider: Compile a portfolio of texts in a range of modes for a common concept, purpose or audience — e.g. a class anthology of poems or stories requiring consistent structural and language decisions across pieces
Create texts in non-traditional forms — scripts for interviews, podcasts, vlogs, digital reflections — selecting conventions appropriate to each form
Use tracked changes in a collaborative editing context to make the decision-making process visible — reflect on editing choices and their effect on meaning
elaborations: compiling a portfolio of texts in a range of modes related to a particular concept, purpose or audience; for example, a class anthology of poems or stories
using appropriate text conventions to create scripts for interviews, presentations, advertisements, radio segments, podcasts, digital and online reflections including vlogs

editing for meaning by removing unnecessary repetition, reordering sentences and varying sentence structures to refine ideas, adding or substituting words for impact, and reviewing accuracy of grammar, spelling and punctuation
tracking a word-processed document to jointly edit texts

AC9E7LY07.minimum_width: Plan and deliver a presentation for a given purpose and audience; use at least one deliberate voice feature (volume, tone, pitch or pace) and explain why it was chosen.
AC9E7LY07.typical_width: Plan, create, rehearse and deliver presentations across at least two purposes; select text structures, language features and visual elements appropriate to the purpose; use voice features deliberately for audience engagement; use peer feedback to refine delivery.
wider: Prepare a presentation combining print, visual and audio elements to explore and interpret ideas, drawing on research about perspectives different from students' own
Monitor ideas at each stage of creating a presentation in a blog or journal — make the planning and revision process explicit
Deliver the same content for two different audiences and reflect on how structural, language and voice choices changed — discuss what the comparison reveals about the audience-purpose relationship
elaborations: preparing a presentation combining print, visual and audio elements to explore and interpret ideas, drawing on knowledge and research about ideas and opinions different from students' own
selecting features of voice, such as tone, volume, pitch and pace, for different audiences and purposes, recognising the effects these have on audience understanding and engagement
monitoring ideas developed at each stage of creating a presentation in a blog or journal
sharing feedback with a peer while planning, creating and rehearsing a presentation

AC9E7LE01.minimum_width: In a given literary text, identify one significant idea, issue or point of view and connect it to the historical, social or cultural context in which the text was created.
AC9E7LE01.typical_width: Identify and explore ideas, points of view, characters, events and issues in literary texts drawn from a range of historical, social and cultural contexts; compare how context shapes what ideas are foregrounded and whose perspective is centred across at least two texts from different contexts.
wider: Explore representations of characters and events in literary texts by First Nations Australians alongside mainstream Australian texts on similar themes — examine what comparison reveals about different perspectives
Explore depictions of the city or the bush in Australian poems and short stories from different eras — discuss how the representation of these settings has changed across historical contexts
Explore how ideas about heroism vary across literary texts by wide-ranging world authors — examine how cultural context shapes what counts as heroic
elaborations: exploring ideas about heroism in literary texts by wide-ranging world authors
discussing the similarities and differences in character representations in film adaptations of novels and plays
exploring representations of characters and events in literary texts by First Nations Australians
exploring depictions of the city or the bush in Australian poems and short stories from different eras

AC9E7LE02.strand: Literature — Engaging with and responding to literature
AC9E7LE02.minimum_width: Form an opinion about a character, setting or event in a given text; justify it with at least one textual reference; identify one point of agreement or difference with another's opinion.
AC9E7LE02.typical_width: Form and justify opinions about characters, settings and events across texts; participate in structured discussion where multiple opinions are present; identify specific points of agreement and difference and respond to interpretive difference by engaging with others' reasoning.
wider: Establish criteria for discussing the relative merits of characters, settings and events before forming opinions — use the criteria to make justification more rigorous and discussable
Discuss texts where characters exhibit morally complex behaviours (integrity, loyalty, moral ambiguity) — examine how different readers can reach different justified conclusions from the same text
Compare personal opinions on First Nations Australian literary texts and wide-ranging world texts on similar themes — discuss how cultural context shapes what readers find persuasive or resonant
elaborations: establishing forums and criteria for discussing the relative merits of characters, settings and events in literary texts
comparing personal opinions on texts and justifying responses in discussions which may include referencing behaviours such as integrity and loyalty

AC9E7LE03.strand: Literature — Engaging with and responding to literature
AC9E7LE03.minimum_width: In a given text, identify one literary device or language feature used to create a character; explain what it reveals about the character; identify one device used to influence the reader's emotions or opinions and explain how.
AC9E7LE03.typical_width: Explain how literary devices and language features — dialogue, description, imagery, visual composition — create character and influence emotions and opinions across at least two text types; explain the mechanisms of influence in each.
wider: Compare the representation of a character's appearance in a novel and a film version of the same text — examine how different media use different devices to construct character
Explain how the same character is presented to generate different reader sympathies in two different texts or adaptations — trace the specific device choices that produce the difference
Examine how literary devices in First Nations Australian texts create character and influence emotions — with attention to how cultural context shapes which devices carry meaning
elaborations: comparing the representation of a character's appearance in a novel and film version of the same text
explaining the impact and significance of language features in a text

AC9E7LE04.strand: Literature — Engaging with and responding to literature
AC9E7LE04.minimum_width: Describe one aspect of aesthetic value and one of social value in a given literary text; use at least two metalanguage terms correctly in doing so.
AC9E7LE04.typical_width: Discuss the aesthetic and social value of literary texts using a range of appropriate metalanguage across both dimensions; determine criteria for evaluating aesthetic value before forming judgements; use specific metalanguage for both film and literary form when comparing an adaptation.
wider: Compare a film adaptation and the source literary text using medium-specific metalanguage — discuss how the aesthetic and social value of each differs and why
Discuss the social value of texts using critical vocabulary (representation, perspective, ideology, context) — explain how metalanguage enables more precise discussion
Evaluate the aesthetic and social value of First Nations Australian literary texts using appropriate metalanguage — discuss how criteria for aesthetic value may be culturally situated
elaborations: determining criteria for evaluating the aesthetic value of a literary text and share opinions

comparing a film adaptation of a literary text using specific language for naming the text structure, literary devices and language features of film and novels, and sharing opinions about the aesthetic and social value of each

AC9E7LE05.minimum_width: In a given narrative, identify how a character, a setting and an event each contribute to meaning; identify one moment where character, setting and event interact to produce meaning together.
AC9E7LE05.typical_width: Explain how characters, settings and events combine to create meaning in narratives — examining how setting shapes character options, how events reveal character, how character choices drive events; analyse how authorial structural choices serve purpose and appeal across at least two narrative texts.
wider: Analyse and explain the structure and features of short stories, discussing the purposes and appeal of different authorial choices for the combination of character, setting and event
Explore traditional stories from Asia and discuss how oral mode, visual elements and verse work alongside character, setting and event to create meaning
Compare how the combination of narrative elements differs between a written story and its film adaptation — examine how the medium affects how the three elements interact
elaborations: analysing and explaining the structure and features of short stories, discussing the purposes and appeal of different authorial choices for structure
exploring traditional stories from Asia and discussing their features; for example, use of the oral mode, visual elements and verse to convey the narrative

AC9E7LE06.minimum_width: In a given text, identify two literary devices using correct metalanguage; explain the effect of each; identify at least two layers of meaning one device creates simultaneously.
AC9E7LE06.typical_width: Explain how literary devices create layers of meaning in poetry and other texts — examining how devices operate on literal, figurative and thematic levels simultaneously; use metalanguage including end and internal rhyme, metre and alliteration accurately in discussion.
wider: Explain the layers of meaning created by imagery in First Nations Australian films, plays and poetry — attend to how cultural and symbolic layers operate alongside the literal
Compare how the same literary device (e.g. imagery of light and dark) creates different layers of meaning in different texts — examine what layers are added or changed by context
Analyse how sound devices (rhyme, alliteration, assonance) create layers of meaning in a poem — explain how the sound layer interacts with the semantic layer
elaborations: explaining the sound and rhythm of poetry using metalanguage; for example, 'end and internal rhyme', 'meter' and 'alliteration', and discussing how layers of meaning are created
viewing or reading First Nations Australian films, plays and poetry, and explaining the layers of meaning created by imagery

AC9E7LE07.minimum_width: Create a literary text that includes one deliberate experiment with a language feature or literary device encountered in reading; identify one editing decision made to improve the effect of that choice.
AC9E7LE07.typical_width: Create and edit literary texts experimenting with at least two language features or literary devices; draw on structures and devices encountered across reading; edit with attention to how each choice is working — what effect is created and what could improve it.
wider: Create a prequel using an imagined series of life events of a character, presented as flashbacks in a scripted monologue — experimenting with temporal structure and narrative voice
Transform a familiar print narrative into a short video or film narrative — make deliberate decisions about how literary devices translate across modes
Experiment with epistolary form, multiple narrators or other structural devices encountered in reading — reflect on what the structural choice makes possible that conventional narrative does not
Draw on devices encountered in First Nations Australian literature — imagery, oral patterns, relational address — and experiment with how they function in a new creative context
elaborations: using aspects of texts in imaginative recreations such as re-situating a character from a text into a new situation
creating a prequel using an imagined series of life events of a character presented as a series of flashbacks in a scripted monologue
creating chapters for an autobiography, short story or diary
experimenting with different narrative structures such as the epistolary form, flashback and multiple narrators
experimenting with imagery, sentence variation, metaphor and word choice when creating a literary text
transforming familiar print narratives into short video or film narratives, drawing on knowledge of the type of text and possible adaptations to setting for a new mode
